claim: An abundant literature reports on 'sequential effects' observed when humans make predictions on the basis of stochastic sequences of stimuli.
source: An abundant literature reports on 'sequential effects' observed when humans make predictions on the basis of stochastic sequences of stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about the existence of literature on sequential effects, supported by the context and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sequential effects represent departures from an optimal, Bayesian process.
source: Such sequential effects represent departures from an optimal, Bayesian process.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of sequential effects in the abstract.

claim: A prominent explanation posits that humans are adapted to changing environments and erroneously assume non-stationarity of the environment even if the latter is static.
source: A prominent explanation posits that humans are adapted to changing environments, and erroneously assume non-stationarity of the environment, even if the latter is static.
evidence: This is presented as an existing explanation in the literature, which is later cited in the introduction.

claim: Sub-optimal and fluctuating predictions result from cognitive constraints (or costs), under which humans behave rationally.
source: We propose a different explanation in which sub-optimal and fluctuating predictions result from cognitive constraints (or costs), under which humans however behave rationally.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the manuscript.

claim: The precision-cost model reproduces a 'repulsive effect' in which predictions are biased away from stimuli presented in more distant trials.
source: Only the precision-cost model reproduces a 'repulsive effect', observed in the data, in which predictions are biased away from stimuli presented in more distant trials.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experimental results and model comparison.

claim: Human reactions were faster when responding to a stimulus whose probability was higher.
source: In the case of choice reaction-time tasks, it was noted in the early 1950s that human reactions were faster when responding to a stimulus whose probability was higher (Hick, 1952; Hyman, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: Faster responses were obtained after a repetition of a stimulus, even in the case of serially-independent stimuli.
source: In addition, faster responses were obtained after a repetition of a stimulus (i.e., when the same stimulus was presented twice in a row), even in the case of serially-independent stimuli (i.e., when the preceding stimulus carried no information on subsequent ones; Hyman, 1953; Bertelson, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies from the 1950s and 1960s.

claim: Studies consistently report a recency effect whereby the more often a simple pattern of stimuli is observed in recent stimulus history, the faster subjects respond to it.
source: These studies consistently report a recency effect whereby the more often a simple pattern of stimuli (e.g. a repetition) is observed in recent stimulus history, the faster subjects respond to it.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Humans may believe that the process generating the stimuli is subject to random changes even when it is in fact constant.
source: A common theoretical account is that humans infer the statistics of the stimuli presented to them, but because they usually live in environments that change over time, they may believe that the process generating the stimuli is subject to random changes even when it is in fact constant (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Wilder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014; Meyniel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical accounts in the literature.

claim: Leaky integration of stimuli has been heuristically modeled as an exponential discounting of past observations.
source: Consequently, they may rely excessively on the most recent stimuli to predict the next ones. In several studies, this was heuristically modeled as a 'leaky integration' of the stimuli, that is, an exponential discounting of past observations (Cho et al., 2002; Yu and Cohen, 2008; Wilder et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2013; Meyniel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple modeling studies.

claim: A cognitive constraint is hindering the inference process and preventing it from converging to the correct, constant belief about the unchanging statistics of the environment.
source: Here, instead of positing that subjects hold an incorrect belief on the dynamics of the environment and do not learn that it is stationary, we propose a different account, whereby a cognitive constraint is hindering the inference process and preventing it from converging to the correct, constant belief about the unchanging statistics of the environment.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed alternative theoretical account.

claim: Under the precision cost hypothesis, more precise posteriors come with higher costs.
source: As for the nature of this cost, we consider two natural hypotheses: first, that a higher precision in belief is harder for subjects to achieve, and thus that more precise posteriors come with higher costs
evidence: This is one of the two hypotheses proposed in the framework.

claim: Under the unpredictability cost hypothesis, unpredictable environments are difficult for subjects to represent and thus entail higher costs.
source: and second, that unpredictable environments are difficult for subjects to represent, and thus that they entail higher costs.
evidence: This is the second hypothesis proposed in the framework.

claim: Under the precision cost hypothesis, the cost is a function of the belief held.
source: Under the first hypothesis, the cost is a function of the belief held, while under the second hypothesis the cost is a function of the inferred environment.
evidence: This distinguishes the two types of costs proposed.

claim: The precision cost predicts 'leaky integration' in which remote observations are discarded.
source: We show that the precision cost predicts 'leaky integration': in the resulting inference process, remote observations are discarded.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the precision cost model.

claim: Under precision cost, beliefs do not converge but fluctuate instead with the recent stimulus history.
source: Crucially, beliefs do not converge but fluctuate instead with the recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the precision cost model.

claim: Under the unpredictability cost, the inference process does converge, although not to the correct (Bayesian) posterior.
source: By contrast, under the unpredictability cost, the inference process does converge, although not to the correct (Bayesian) posterior, but rather to a posterior that implies a biased belief on the temporal structure of the stimuli.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the unpredictability cost model.

claim: The stimulus generative probability was manipulated in separate blocks of trials to span the range from 0.05 to 0.95 by increments of 0.05.
source: We thus manipulate in separate blocks of trials the stimulus generative probability (i.e., the Bernoulli probability that parameterizes the stimulus) to span the range from 0.05 to 0.95 by increments of 0.05.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Subjects' predictions depend on the stimulus generative probability.
source: We found that subjects' predictions depend on both the stimulus generative probability and the recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Subjects' predictions depend on the history of stimuli.
source: We found that subjects' predictions depend on both the stimulus generative probability and the recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The occurrence of a stimulus in past trials increases the proportion of predictions identical to this stimulus (attractive effect).
source: We examine whether the occurrence of a stimulus, in past trials, increase the proportion of predictions identical to this stimulus ('attractive effect'), or whether it decreases this proportion ('repulsive effect').
evidence: This defines the attractive effect observed in the data.

claim: The responses of subjects exhibit an elaborate pattern of attractive and repulsive effects.
source: We show that the responses of subjects exhibit an elaborate, and at times counter-intuitive, pattern of attractive and repulsive effects
evidence: This summarizes the experimental findings.

claim: The brain infers a stimulus generative probability under a constraint on the precision of its internal representations.
source: Our results suggest that the brain infers a stimulus generative probability, but under a constraint on the precision of its internal representations
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results and model comparison.

claim: The inferred generative process may include higher-order statistics (e.g. transition probabilities), in contrast with the Bernoulli-distributed stimulus used in the experiment.
source: the inferred generative process may be more general than the actual one, and include higher-order statistics (e.g. transition probabilities), in contrast with the Bernoulli-distributed stimulus used in the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: The preceding stimulus has an 'attractive' sequential effect.
source: In other words, the preceding stimulus has an 'attractive' sequential effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental finding that p̄(A|A) > p̄(A|B).

claim: As more evidence is accumulated, the Bayesian posterior gradually narrows and converges towards the value of the stimulus generative probability.
source: As more evidence is accumulated, the Bayesian posterior gradually narrows and converges towards the value of the stimulus generative probability (Figure 3c and d, grey lines).
evidence: This is a well-known property of Bayesian inference, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Wider (less concentrated) distributions are less costly than narrower (more concentrated) distributions under the precision cost.
source: Wider (less concentrated) distributions provide less information about the probability parameter and are thus less costly than narrower (more concentrated) distributions (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a consequence of the precision cost definition, illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The precision cost model recovers the predictions of leaky-integration models.
source: Specifically, we recover the predictions of leaky-integration models, in which remote patterns in the sequence of stimuli are discounted through an exponential filter (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Meyniel et al., 2016); here, we do not posit the gradual forgetting of remote observations, but instead we derive it as an optimal solution to a problem of constrained inference.
evidence: This is a theoretical result showing equivalence to existing models, supported by citations.

claim: For a Bernoulli observer, a posterior concentrated on extreme values of the Bernoulli parameter comes with a lower unpredictability cost than a posterior concentrated on values close to 0.5.
source: For a Bernoulli observer, a posterior concentrated on extreme values of the Bernoulli parameter (toward 0 or 1), thus representing more predictable environments, comes with a lower cost than a posterior concentrated on values of the Bernoulli parameter close to 0.5, which correspond to the most unpredictable environments (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a consequence of the unpredictability cost definition, illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: With the unpredictability cost, except in the equiprobable case, the inference converges but it is biased.
source: In other words, except in the equiprobable case, the inference converges but it is biased, i.e., the posterior peaks at an incorrect value of the stimulus generative probability (Figure 3c and d, green lines).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: With the unpredictability cost, the biased value is closer to the extremes (0 and 1) than the stimulus generative probability.
source: This value is closer to the extremes (0 and 1) than the stimulus generative probability, that is, it implies an environment more predictable than the actual one (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 3d.

claim: With the unpredictability cost for Markov observers, the prediction of the next stimulus being A depends on whether the preceding stimulus was A or B, predicting sequential effects.
source: The prediction of the next stimulus being A on a given trial depends on whether the preceding stimulus was A or B: this model therefore predicts sequential effects.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the unpredictability cost model for Markov observers.

claim: 60% of subjects are best fitted by one of the unpredictability-cost models.
source: We find that 60% of subjects are best fitted by one of the unpredictability-cost models, while 40% are best fitted by one of the precision-cost models.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: 65% of subjects are best fitted by a Markov-observer model.
source: When pooling the two types of cost, 65% of subjects are best fitted by a Markov-observer model.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: The expected probability of unpredictability-cost models is 57% with an exceedance probability of 78%.
source: The derived expected probability of unpredictability-cost models is 57% (and 43% for precision-cost models) with an exceedance probability (i.e. probability that unpredictability-cost models are more frequent in the general population) of 78%.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian model selection procedure.

claim: The expected probability of Markov-observer models is 70% with an exceedance probability of 98%.
source: The expected probability of Markov-observer models, regardless of the cost used in the model, is 70% (and 30% for Bernoulli-observer models) with an exceedance probability (i.e. probability that Markov-observer models are more frequent in the general population) of 98%.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian model selection procedure.

claim: The responses of subjects are generally consistent with a Markov-observer model.
source: These results indicate that the responses of subjects are generally consistent with a Markov-observer model, although the stimuli used in the experiment are Bernoulli-distributed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model selection results.

claim: Bayesian model selection does not provide decisive evidence in favor of either the unpredictability-cost or precision-cost family of models.
source: As for the unpredictability-cost and the precision-cost families of models, Bayesian model selection does not provide decisive evidence in favor of either model, indicating that they both capture some aspects of the responses of the subjects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model selection results.

claim: The best-fitting model corresponds to the true model in at least 70% of simulations in the confusion matrix analysis.
source: We find that the best-fitting model corresponds to the true model in at least 70% of simulations (the chance level is 12.5%=1/8 models), and actually more than 90% for the majority of models
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis of the model-fitting procedure.

claim: With the unpredictability-cost model of a Bernoulli observer, after 200 passive trials, the model predicts practically no sequential effects.
source: After the 200 stimuli of the passive trials, the sequential effects of the most recent stimulus resulting from this transient regime appear small in comparison to the sequential effects obtained with the other models (Figure 7b, first row).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 7b.

claim: Both families of costs are able to produce attractive sequential effects.
source: Both families of costs are thus able to produce attractive sequential effects, albeit with some qualitative differences.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical predictions from both model families.

claim: The precision-cost models are slightly better than the unpredictability-cost models at capturing the behavior of subjects that they do not best fit.
source: The precision-cost models, however, seem slightly better than the unpredictability-cost models at capturing the behavior of the subjects that they do not best fit (Figure 4, compare panel j to panel f, and panel i to panel e).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing panels in Figure 4.

claim: With unpredictability-cost models, when m≥n, the sequential effects are attractive.
source: In this case, the sequential effects are attractive (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The occurrence of A as the third-to-last stimulus increases the proportion of the opposite prediction B when followed by BA.
source: Thus, in these cases, the occurrence of A as the third-to-last stimulus increases (in comparison with the occurrence of a B) the proportion of the opposite prediction, B.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the repulsive effect finding.

claim: For subjects best fitted by unpredictability-cost models, there is also a significant repulsive effect of the third-to-last stimulus when followed by BA.
source: For the subjects best fitted by the unpredictability-cost models (a family of model that does not predict any repulsive sequential effects), we also find, perhaps surprisingly, a significant repulsive effect of the third-to-last stimulus (p-values <0.01 for three probabilities, <0.05 for five probabilities; subjects pooled), which demonstrates the robustness of this effect (Figure 6e, right panel).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Regardless of the model that best fits their overall predictions, the behavior of subjects is consistent only with the precision-cost family of models with Markov order ≥1.
source: Thus, in spite of the results of the model-selection procedure, some sequential effects in subjects' predictions support only one of the two families of model. Regardless of the model that best fits their overall predictions, the behavior of the subjects is consistent only with the precision-cost family of models with Markov order equal to or greater than 1, that is, with a model of inference of conditional probabilities hampered by a cognitive cost weighing on the precision of belief distributions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of higher-order sequential effects.

claim: Sequential effects in human predictions result from cognitive constraints hindering the inference process carried out by the brain.
source: We investigated the hypothesis that sequential effects in human predictions result from cognitive constraints hindering the inference process carried out by the brain.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: The proportion of forced-choice predictions for a given stimulus should increase with the stimulus generative probability according to the models.
source: First, the proportion of forced-choice predictions for a given stimulus should increase with the stimulus generative probability.
evidence: This is a prediction from the models.

claim: Most models predict sequential effects where predictions depend on the recent stimulus history.
source: Second, most of those models predict sequential effects: predictions also depend on the recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is a prediction from the models.

claim: Models with different types of cognitive cost resulted in different patterns of attractive and repulsive effects.
source: Models with different types of cognitive cost resulted in different patterns of attractive and repulsive effects of the past few stimuli on predictions.
evidence: This is a finding from the theoretical analysis of the models.

claim: Subjects' predictions depend on both the stimulus generative probability and the recent stimulus history.
source: We found that subjects' predictions depend on both the stimulus generative probability and the recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Sequential effects exhibited both attractive and repulsive components which were modulated by the stimulus generative probability.
source: Sequential effects exhibited both attractive and repulsive components which were modulated by the stimulus generative probability.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The behavior was qualitatively accounted for by a model of constrained inference in which the subject infers transition probabilities and bears a cost that increases with the precision of the posterior distributions.
source: This behavior was qualitatively accounted for by a model of constrained inference in which the subject infers the transition probabilities underlying the sequences of stimuli and bears a cost that increases with the precision of the posterior distributions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The notion that human decisions can be understood as resulting from a constrained optimization has gained traction across several fields.
source: The notion that human decisions can be understood as resulting from a constrained optimization has gained traction across several fields, including neuroscience, cognitive science, and economics.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of the research, supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Theories of 'efficient coding' account for the bias and the variability of perception.
source: related theories of 'efficient coding' account for the bias and the variability of perception (Ganguli and Simoncelli, 2016; Wei and Stocker, 2015; Wei and Stocker, 2017; Prat-Carrabin and Woodford, 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Herbert Simon defines bounded rationality as 'rational choice that takes into account the cognitive limitations of the decision maker'.
source: In cognitive science and economics, 'bounded rationality' is a precursory concept introduced in the 1950s by Herbert Simon, who defines it as "rational choice that takes into account the cognitive limitations of the decision maker — limitations of both knowledge and computational capacity" (Simon, 1997).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Simon (1997).

claim: The 'resource-rational analysis' paradigm aims at a unified theoretical account that reconciles principles of rationality with realistic constraints about the resources available to the brain.
source: The 'resource-rational analysis' paradigm aims at a unified theoretical account that reconciles principles of rationality with realistic constraints about the resources available to the brain when it is carrying out computations (Griffiths et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Griffiths et al., 2015.

claim: In the resource-rational approach, biases result from the constraints on resources, rather than from 'simple heuristics'.
source: In this approach, biases result from the constraints on resources, rather than from 'simple heuristics' (see Lieder and Griffiths, 2019 for an extensive review).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lieder and Griffiths, 2019.

claim: Traditional accounts attribute sequential effects to a belief in sequential dependencies between successive outcomes.
source: Traditional accounts since the 1960s attribute these effects to a belief in sequential dependencies between successive outcomes (Edwards, 1961; Matthews and Sanders, 1984) (potentially 'acquired through life experience' Ayton and Fischer, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Models in which subjects carry out statistical inference assuming that parameters are subject to changes have been proposed to formalize traditional accounts of sequential effects.
source: This traditional account was formalized, in particular, by models in which subjects carry out a statistical inference about the sequence of stimuli presented to them, and this inference assumes that the parameters underlying the generating process are subject to changes (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Wilder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014; Meyniel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Human subjects dynamically adapt their learning rate when the environment changes.
source: Human subjects indeed dynamically adapt their learning rate when the environment changes (Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017; Nassar et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Subjects can adapt their inference to the statistics of changes in the environment.
source: and they can even adapt their inference to the statistics of these changes (Behrens et al., 2007; Prat-Carrabin et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In the task and many previous studies, the underlying statistics are not changing across trials.
source: However, in our task and in many previous studies in which sequential effects have been reported, the underlying statistics are in fact not changing across trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Many previous studies on biased belief updating have proposed models with different exponents applied to the prior and to the likelihood.
source: Many previous studies on biased belief updating have proposed models that adopt the same form except for the different exponents applied to the prior and to the likelihood (Grether, 1980; Matsumori et al., 2018; Benjamin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: With the precision cost, both the prior and likelihood are raised to the same exponent, and the inference amounts to an exponentially decaying count of observed patterns.
source: Here, with the precision cost, both quantities are raised to the same exponent and we note that in this case the inference of the subject amounts to an exponentially decaying count of the patterns observed in the sequence of stimuli, which is sometimes called 'leaky integration' in the literature (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Wilder et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2013; Meyniel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical result with citations to related literature.

claim: Models that posit a belief in changing statistics are well approximated by models of leaky integration.
source: The models mentioned above, that posit a belief in changing statistics, indeed are well approximated by models of leaky integration (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Meyniel et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The minimization of a loss function formalizes a trade-off between the distance to optimality of the inference and the cognitive constraints.
source: In our modeling approach, the minimization of a loss function (Equation 1) formalizes a trade-off between the distance to optimality of the inference, and the cognitive constraints under which it is carried out.
evidence: This is an explanation of the theoretical framework.

claim: The proposal is not that the brain actively solves the optimization problem online, but that it is endowed with an inference algorithm which is effectively a solution to the constrained optimization problem.
source: We stress that our proposal is not that the brain actively solves this optimization problem online, but instead that it is endowed with an inference algorithm (whose origin remains to be elucidated) which is effectively a solution to the constrained optimization problem.
evidence: This clarifies the interpretation of the theoretical framework.

claim: The intuitive assumption that it is costly to be precise finds a more concrete realization in neural models of inference with probabilistic population codes.
source: The intuitive assumption that it is costly to be precise finds a more concrete realization in neural models of inference with probabilistic population codes: in these models, the precision of the posterior is proportional to the average activity of the population of neurons and to the number of neurons (Ma et al., 2006; Seung and Sompolinsky, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neural modeling studies.

claim: More neural activity and more neurons arguably come with a metabolic cost, and thus more precise posteriors are more costly in neural models.
source: More neural activity and more neurons arguably come with a metabolic cost, and thus more precise posteriors are more costly in these models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the neural models cited.

claim: Imprecisions in computations successfully account for decision variability and adaptive behavior in volatile environments.
source: Imprecisions in computations, moreover, was shown to successfully account for decision variability and adaptive behavior in volatile environments (Findling et al., 2019; Findling et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The brain may run stochastic simulations of implied environments, as proposed in models of 'intuitive physics' and 'simulation heuristics'.
source: This could be the case, for instance, under the hypothesis that the brain runs stochastic simulations of the implied environments, as proposed in models of 'intuitive physics' (Battaglia et al., 2013) and in Kahneman and Tversky's 'simulation heuristics' (Kahneman et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cognitive models.

claim: More entropic environments imply more possible scenarios to simulate, giving rise to higher costs under the simulation hypothesis.
source: More entropic environments imply more possible scenarios to simulate, giving rise, under this assumption, to higher costs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation hypothesis.

claim: The brain may carry out a mental compression of sequences, and entropy is a measure of the degree of compressibility.
source: A different literature explores the hypothesis that the brain carries out a mental compression of sequences (Simon, 1972; Chekaf et al., 2016; Planton et al., 2021); entropy in this context is a measure of the degree of compressibility of a sequence (Planton et al., 2021), and thus, presumably, of its implied cost.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mental compression.

claim: Human subjects exhibit a preference for predictive information.
source: Human subjects exhibit a preference for predictive information indeed (Ogawa and Watanabe, 2011; Trapp et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Unpredictable stimuli increase anxiety-like behavior and induce more neural activity.
source: while unpredictable stimuli have been shown not only to increase anxiety-like behavior (Herry et al., 2007), but also to induce more neural activity (Herry et al., 2007; den Ouden et al., 2009; Alink et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience studies.

claim: Both precision and unpredictability costs can predict sequential effects without an explicit assumption that presupposes their existence.
source: We note that both costs (precision and unpredictability) can predict sequential effects, even though neither carries ex ante an explicit assumption that presupposes the existence of sequential effects.
evidence: This is an observation about the theoretical properties of the models.

claim: Both cost types reproduce the attractive recency effect of the last stimulus exhibited by the subjects.
source: They both reproduce the attractive recency effect of the last stimulus exhibited by the subjects.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The two cost types make quantitatively different predictions, and this diversity of behaviors is found in subjects.
source: They make quantitatively different predictions (Figure 4); we also find this diversity of behaviors in subjects.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The psychology and neuroscience literature proposes many 'leaky integrators' or 'leaky accumulators' models.
source: The psychology and neuroscience literature proposes many similar 'leaky integrators' or 'leaky accumulators' models (Smith, 1995; Roe et al., 2001; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Cook and Maunsell, 2002; Wang, 2002; Sugrue et al., 2004; Bogacz et al., 2006; Kiani et al., 2008; Yu and Cohen, 2008; Gao et al., 2011; Tsetsos et al., 2012; Ossmy et al., 2013; Meyniel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to the literature.

claim: In connectionist models of decision-making, decision units have activity levels that accumulate evidence and decay to zero in the absence of input.
source: In connectionist models of decision-making, for instance, decision units in abstract network models have activity levels that accumulate evidence received from input units, and which decay to zero in the absence of input (Roe et al., 2001; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Wang, 2002; Bogacz et al., 2006; Tsetsos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectionist models.

claim: In the authors' approach, leaky integration is not an assumption about mechanisms but an optimal strategy in the face of a cognitive cost weighing on the precision of beliefs.
source: In our approach, leaky integration is not an assumption about the mechanisms underpinning some cognitive process: instead, we find that it is an optimal strategy in the face of a cognitive cost weighing on the precision of beliefs.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical contribution of the study.

claim: The majority of studies on sequential effects have focused on equiprobable Bernoulli environments where both stimuli had probability 0.5.
source: Turning to the experimental results, we note that in spite of the rich literature on sequential effects, the majority of studies have focused on equiprobable Bernoulli environments, in which the two possible stimuli both had a probability equal to 0.5, as in tosses of a fair coin (Soetens et al., 1985; Cho et al., 2002; Yu and Cohen, 2008; Wilder et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Ayton and Fischer, 2004; Gökaydin and Ejova, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In equiprobable environments, the two stimuli play symmetric roles and all sequences of a given length are equally probable.
source: In environments of this kind, the two stimuli play symmetric roles and all sequences of a given length are equally probable.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of equiprobable environments.

claim: In biased environments, one of the two possible stimuli is more probable than the other.
source: In contrast, in biased environments one of the two possible stimuli is more probable than the other.
evidence: This is a definition of biased environments.

claim: The finding that the proportion of prediction A is more extreme than the stimulus generative probability is consistent with observations by Edwards and with conclusions of a more recent review.
source: This result is consistent with the observations made by Edwards, 1961; Edwards, 1956 and with the conclusions of a more recent review (Vulkan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recency effects are common in the psychology literature and have been reported from memory to causal learning to inference.
source: In addition to varying with the stimulus generative probability, the subjects' predictions depend on the recent history of stimuli. Recency effects are common in the psychology literature; they were reported from memory (Ebbinghaus et al., 1913) to causal learning (Collins and Shanks, 2002) to inference (Shanteau, 1972; Hogarth and Einhorn, 1992; Benjamin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies across different domains.

claim: Both attractive recency effects ('hot-hand fallacy') and repulsive recency effects ('gambler's fallacy') have been reported in prediction tasks.
source: In prediction tasks (like ours), both attractive recency effects, also called 'hot-hand fallacy', and repulsive recency effects, also called 'gambler's fallacy', have been reported (Jarvik, 1951; Edwards, 1961; Ayton and Fischer, 2004; Burns and Corpus, 2004; Croson and Sundali, 2005; Oskarsson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The observation of both attractive and repulsive effects within the same experiment has been reported in a visual identification task and in risky choices.
source: The observation of both effects within the same experiment has been reported in a visual identification task (Chopin and Mamassian, 2012) and in risky choices ('wavy recency effect' Plonsky et al., 2015; Plonsky and Erev, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two important factors for the heterogeneity of recency effect results are the perceived degree of randomness of the predicted variable and whether it relates to human performance.
source: As to the heterogeneity of these results, several explanations have been proposed; two important factors seem to be the perceived degree of randomness of the predicted variable and whether it relates to human performance (Ayton and Fischer, 2004; Burns and Corpus, 2004; Croson and Sundali, 2005; Oskarsson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Edwards concluded to an attractive recency effect ('probability following') in a task similar to the authors' task.
source: With this analysis, Edwards (Edwards, 1961) in a task similar to ours concluded to an attractive recency effect (which he called 'probability following').
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Edwards, 1961.

claim: The authors provide a more detailed picture of the influence of each stimulus preceding the prediction, revealing a non-trivial finer structure of recency effects.
source: Although our results are consistent with this observation (in our data three As in a row do increase the proportion of predictions A), we provide a more detailed picture of the influence of each stimulus preceding the prediction, whether it is in a 'run' of identical stimuli or not, which allows us to exhibit the non-trivial finer structure of the recency effects that is often overlooked.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the study.

claim: Wilder et al., 2009, Jones et al., 2013, and Meyniel et al., 2016 argue that sequential effects result from an imperfect inference of the base rate and of the frequency of repetitions and alternations.
source: Wilder et al., 2009, Jones et al., 2013, and Meyniel et al., 2016 similarly argue that sequential effects result from an imperfect inference of the base rate and of the frequency of repetitions and alternations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dehaene et al., 2015 argue that the knowledge of transition probabilities is a central mechanism in the brain's processing of sequences.
source: Dehaene et al., 2015 argue that the knowledge of transition probabilities is a central mechanism in the brain's processing of sequences (e.g. in language comprehension)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dehaene et al., 2015.

claim: Infants as young as 5 months were shown to be able to track both base rates and transition probabilities.
source: and infants as young as 5 months were shown to be able to track both base rates and transition probabilities (see Saffran and Kirkham, 2018 for a review).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review by Saffran and Kirkham, 2018.

claim: Learning of transition probabilities has been observed in rhesus monkeys.
source: Learning of transition probabilities has also been observed in rhesus monkeys (Meyer and Olson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meyer and Olson, 2011.

claim: Human performance in various inference tasks is often suboptimal.
source: In spite of the success of the Bayesian framework, we note that human performance in various inference tasks is often suboptimal (Nassar et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2013; Acerbi et al., 2014; Prat-Carrabin et al., 2021b; Prat-Carrabin and Woodford, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The deviations from optimality in inference tasks may be explained by the cognitive constraints at play in the inference carried out by humans.
source: Our approach suggests that the deviations from optimality in these tasks may be explained by the cognitive constraints at play in the inference carried out by humans.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the theoretical framework of the study.

claim: Kominers et al., 2016 consider a model in which Bayesian inference comes with a fixed cost and the observer can choose to forgo updating her belief.
source: Kominers et al., 2016 consider a model in which Bayesian inference comes with a fixed cost; the observer can choose to forgo updating her belief, so as to avoid the cost.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kominers et al., 2016.

claim: The model by Kominers et al., 2016 predicts 'permanently cycling beliefs' in some cases.
source: In some cases, the model predicts 'permanently cycling beliefs' that do not converge
evidence: This is a prediction from the model by Kominers et al., 2016.

claim: The significant sequential effects found in subjects' responses indicate that they are sensitive to both unsurprising and surprising observations.
source: The significant sequential effects we find in our subjects' responses, however, seem to indicate that they are sensitive to both unsurprising (e.g. outcome A when p>0.5) and surprising (outcome B when p>0.5) observations, at least across the values of the stimulus generative probability that we test (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Graeber, 2020 considers costly information processing as an account of subjects' neglect of confounding variables but concludes that suboptimal behavior results from misunderstanding of the information structure.
source: Graeber, 2020 considers costly information processing as an account of subjects' neglect of confounding variables in an inference task, but concludes instead that the suboptimal behavior of subjects results from their misunderstanding of the information structure in the task.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Graeber, 2020.

claim: A model close to the authors' is proposed in Azeredo da Silveira and Woodford, 2019 and Azeredo da Silveira et al., 2020, in which an information-theoretic cost limits memory.
source: A model close to ours is the one proposed in Azeredo da Silveira and Woodford, 2019 and Azeredo da Silveira et al., 2020, in which an information-theoretic cost limits the memory of an otherwise optimal and Bayesian decision-maker, resulting, here also, in beliefs that fluctuate and do not converge, and in an overweighting, in decisions, of the recent evidence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to related models.

claim: Dasgupta et al., 2020 implement a neural network that learns to approximate Bayesian posteriors with constraints from network structure and parameter sharing across problems.
source: Taking a different approach, Dasgupta et al., 2020 implement a neural network that learns to approximate Bayesian posteriors. Possible approximate posteriors are constrained not only by the structure of the network, but also by the fact that the same network is used to address a series of different inference problems. Thus the network's parameters must be 'shared' across problems, which is meant to capture the brain's limited computational resources.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dasgupta et al., 2020.

claim: Minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence allows the model subject to obtain a posterior as close as possible to the optimal posterior.
source: Minimizing this divergence (under a cost) allows the model subject to obtain a posterior as close as possible (at least by this measure) to the optimal posterior given the most recent stimulus and the subject's belief prior to observing the stimulus, which in turn enables the subject to perform reasonably well in the task.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for using the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

claim: Rewarding subjects with a higher payoff for correct predictions would change the optimal trade-off, resulting in 'better' posteriors closer to the Bayesian posterior.
source: In principle, rewarding subjects with a higher payoff when they make a correct prediction would change the optimal trade-off (between the distance to the optimal posterior and the cognitive costs) formalized in Equation 1, resulting in 'better' posteriors (closer to the Bayesian posterior), and thus to higher performance in the task.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the effect of incentivization.

claim: Incentivization is known to influence the extent to which choice behavior is close to probability matching.
source: At the same time, incentivization is known to influence, also in the direction of higher performance, the extent to which choice behavior is close to probability matching (Vulkan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vulkan, 2000.

claim: The approach of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the optimal posterior to the approximate posterior is widely used in machine learning and forms the basis of 'variational' approximate-inference techniques.
source: In any case, the approach of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the optimal posterior to the approximate posterior is widely used in the machine learning literature, and forms the basis of the 'variational' family of approximate-inference techniques (Bishop, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bishop, 2006.

claim: Variational inference techniques have inspired various cognitive models.
source: These techniques have inspired various cognitive models (Sanborn, 2017; Gallistel and Latham, 2022; Aridor and Woodford, 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to cognitive models.

claim: A bound on the divergence, known as the 'evidence bound' or negative 'free energy', is maximized in neuroscience models.
source: alternatively, a bound on the divergence, known as the 'evidence bound', or, in neuroscience, as the negative of the 'free energy', is maximized (Moustafa, 2017; Friston et al., 2006; Friston, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience models.

claim: In variational techniques, the approximate posterior is chosen within a convenient family of tractable, parameterized distributions.
source: In these techniques, the approximate posterior is chosen within a convenient family of tractable, parameterized distributions; other distributions are precluded.
evidence: This is a description of variational inference techniques.

claim: The precision cost and the unpredictability cost are 'smooth' and allow for any distribution but penalize certain types of distributions.
source: The precision cost and the unpredictability cost, in comparison, are 'smooth', and allow for any distribution, but they penalize, respectively, more precise belief distributions, and belief distributions that imply more unpredictable environments.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' costs to variational inference.

claim: Inference subject to either precision or unpredictability cost yields an attractive sequential effect of the most recent observation.
source: Our study shows that inference, when subject to either of these costs, yields an attractive sequential effect of the most recent observation
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical findings.

claim: Twenty subjects (7 women, 13 men; age: 18–41, mean 25.5, standard deviation 6.2) participated in the experiment.
source: Twenty subjects (7 women, 13 men; age: 18–41, mean 25.5, standard deviation 6.2) participated in the experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: All subjects completed the ten blocks of trials, except one subject who did not finish the experiment and was excluded from the analysis.
source: All subjects completed the ten blocks of trials, except one subject who did not finish the experiment and was excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This describes the data collection and exclusion criteria.

source: The study was approved by the ethics committee Île de France VII (CPP 08–021).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants gave their written consent prior to participating.
source: Participants gave their written consent prior to participating.
evidence: This is a statement about informed consent.

claim: Trials in which subjects failed to respond within the limit of 1 s represented 1.27% of the trials on average.
source: The trials in which subjects failed to respond within the limit of 1 s were not included in the analysis. They represented 1.27% of the trials, on average (across subjects); and for 95% of the subjects these trials represented less than 2.5% of the trials.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the data.
